entries.gloss: kn at the start of a word: the k is silent (nyfe, nee)
the l is silent in half, calm, talk, walk, folk
the h is silent: AH-nist, OW-er; so 'an honest', 'an hour'
THOH: here -ough sounds like 'oh', as in although, dough
THROO: here -ough sounds like 'oo'; the same sound as threw
-ought sounds like 'awt': thawt, bawt; the gh is silent
here -ough sounds like 'uff': tuff, ruff, ih-NUFF
BIZ-nis: two syllables; the u sounds like i, the middle i is silent
MIN-it (sixty seconds) vs. my-NOOT (very small, very detailed)
leed (to guide, be first) vs. led (the heavy metal, lead pipes)
reed in the present; red in the past and past participle
liv (to live) vs. lyve (a live show, live data)
klohss with s (near, a close friend) vs. klohz with z (to shut)
SED and SEZ with a short e; not 'sayd' or 'sayz'
unstressed -age at the end is said ij: MES-ij, VIL-ij, IM-ij
-ture is said cher: NAY-cher, KUL-cher; not 'na-toor'
mb at the end of a word: the b is silent (klyme, thum)
b before t is silent: det, dowt; also in debtor, doubtful
t after s before -en or -le is silent: LIS-un, KAS-ul
EYE-lund: the s is silent; also in isle and aisle
AN-ser: the w is silent, as in sword and two
FOR-in: the g is silent, as in sign and reign
BIZ-ee: the u sounds like the i in 'is'
HURD, rhymes with 'word'; not like 'hear' plus d
NAH-lij: silent k; the vowel is ah, not the oh of know
teer (a drop from the eye) vs. tair (to rip)
yooss with s (a use, no use) vs. yooz with z (to use)
wind with a short i (moving air) vs. wynd (turn, wind a clock)

entries.term: ch as k: character, stomach, technique
entries.gloss: in many Greek-origin words ch sounds like k: KAIR-ik-ter, STUM-uk

entries.term: ou as uh: country, double, cousin
entries.gloss: ou often sounds like the u in 'cup': KUN-tree, DUB-ul

entries.term: o as uh: among, oven, government
entries.gloss: o sounds like the u in 'cup': uh-MUNG, UV-un, GUV-ern-ment
one weak syllable usually drops: EV-ree, DIF-runt, FAM-lee

entries.term: g as j: logic, register, technology
entries.gloss: g before e, i, y is often j: LAH-jik, REJ-is-ter; not a hard g

entries.term: x as gz: exact, example, exist
entries.gloss: x before a stressed vowel is gz: ig-ZAKT, ig-ZAM-pul
-sion is zhun after a vowel (decision), shun after s or l (mission)
-ate in nouns and adjectives is a weak 'it': KLY-mit, PRY-vit
-ine has three sounds: EN-jin, muh-SHEEN, dih-FYNE
wr at the start: the w is silent (ryte, rawng)

entries.term: wh as h: who, whole, whose
entries.gloss: these words start with an h sound; the w is silent

entries.term: ea as e: head, bread, health
entries.gloss: ea is a short e in head, bread, health, weather; not ee

entries.term: o as oo: move, prove, whom
entries.gloss: o sounds like oo here: moov, proov, hoom; not a German o

entries.term: ea as ay: great, break, steak
entries.gloss: ea sounds like ay here, not ee: grayt, brayk, stayk
eigh is ay in weight and eight, but eye in height
laugh has laf; daughter, caught, taught have aw; gh is silent
KAWF: here -ough sounds like 'off'; also trough
DEZ-ert (dry land) vs. dih-ZURT (sweet course): different stress and sound
chooz (present) vs. chohz (past); both end in a z sound
MUSS-ul: the c is silent, as in scissors and scene
sign has a silent g (syne); in signature the g is said
final -mn: the n is silent (AW-tum, KAH-lum, kun-DEM)

parts.title: Word stress, sentence stress and intonation
parts.deck: kizamu-english::C1::09 Pronunciation::03 Word stress, sentence stress and intonation

entries.gloss: stress the syllable just before -ic or -ical: sy-un-TIF-ik, TEK-nih-kul
stress the syllable before -logy or -graphy: by-AH-luh-jee, jee-AH-gruh-fee

entries.term: contrastive stress: I said blue, not green
entries.gloss: stress the word you correct or contrast; it gets the strongest beat
the last new, important word in a phrase gets the main stress
normal wh-questions fall at the end: Where do you work?
yes/no questions usually rise at the end: Do you work here?
a falling tag expects agreement: It's cold, isn't it?
a rising tag asks a real question: You're coming, aren't you?
rise on each item, fall on the last: apples, pears, and plums
speak in short meaningful chunks with small pauses between them
unstressed was and were reduce to wuz and wer: it wuz fine

entries.term: weak have / has in perfect tenses
entries.gloss: unstressed auxiliary have reduces to uv or 've: the kids uv left

entries.term: strong forms at the end: Where are you from?
entries.gloss: small words keep their full vowel at the end: from, to, at
STRAT-uh-jee: stress on the first syllable, not German stra-te-GIE
THEER-ee stresses the first syllable, but thee-uh-RET-ih-kul: the stress moves
-ee usually takes the main stress: tray-NEE, gair-un-TEE, ref-uh-REE
-eer always takes the main stress: en-juh-NEER, vah-lun-TEER
stress the syllable just before these endings: fuh-NAN-shul, myoo-ZISH-un
-ique takes the stress and sounds like 'eek': tek-NEEK, yoo-NEEK
stress two syllables before -ate: KAHN-sun-trayt, DEM-un-strayt

entries.term: two-syllable nouns vs. verbs: the basic rule
entries.gloss: most two-syllable nouns stress the first syllable, most verbs the second

entries.term: prefixes: stress on the root: unhappy, rewrite
entries.gloss: prefixes like un-, re-, dis- are usually unstressed: un-HAP-ee, ree-RYTE
compound adjectives usually stress the second part: well-KNOWN, long-TERM
the article a is a short uh, not ay: uh book, un apple
unstressed are reduces to er: What er you doing?
unstressed at reduces to ut: look ut this, ut the office
unstressed from reduces to frum: a letter frum the bank
unstressed some (an amount) reduces to sum: I need sum water
already mentioned words lose stress; the stress moves to the new word
rise on the first choice, fall on the last: tea (rise) or coffee (fall)?
a statement with rising intonation works as a surprised question
repeat with a wh-word and a sharp rise to show surprise or ask again
fall-rise signals a reservation or an unsaid 'but': The talk was good…
rising Sorry? asks someone to repeat; falling Sorry. apologizes

entries.term: flat intonation sounds bored or rude
entries.gloss: English uses wide pitch movement; a flat voice sounds uninterested or unfriendly

entries.term: street names: Main Street vs. Main Avenue
entries.gloss: Street is never stressed (MAIN Street); Avenue, Road, Drive are (Main AVenue)
KAHN-sept: stress on the first syllable, unlike German Konzept
KAHN-tekst: stress on the first syllable; contextual is kun-TEKS-choo-ul
EK-spert: stress on the first syllable; German Experte stresses the second
fuh-LAH-suh-fee: stress on the second syllable, not on the end
FIZ-iks: stress on the first syllable, not German Physik
AT-mus-feer: stress on the first syllable, not German Atmosphäre
MEK-uh-niz-um: stress on the first syllable; the ch sounds like k
kuh-TAS-truh-fee: four syllables, stress on the second
yur-uh-PEE-un: stress on -pe-, not yoo-ROH-pee-un
PROH-gram: stress on the first syllable; programmer is PROH-gram-er
PREZ-ih-dent: stress on the first syllable; presidential is prez-ih-DEN-shul
MOH-ment: stress on the first syllable, unlike German Moment
US REE-sorss: stress usually on the first syllable
kuh-REER (stress on the end) vs. KAIR-ee-er (stress on the start)

entries.term: past simple with a finished time: I saw it yesterday
entries.gloss: a finished time like yesterday, last year or in 2019 needs the past simple

entries.term: present perfect for life experience: Have you ever been to Japan?
entries.gloss: experience at some time up to now, with no time given

entries.term: When-questions in the past simple: When did you arrive?
entries.gloss: when asks about a finished time, so it takes the past simple, not have

entries.term: present perfect for unfinished states: I've known her for years
entries.gloss: a state that began in the past and continues now: know, live, be

entries.term: How long have you …?: How long have you lived here?
entries.gloss: asks about duration up to now; not 'How long do you live here?'

entries.term: It's been … since: It's been two years since we met
entries.gloss: says how much time has passed since an event

entries.term: US past simple with just, already and yet: Did you eat yet?
entries.gloss: American speech often uses the past simple where British English uses the present perfect

entries.term: been vs. gone: She's been to Paris / She's gone to Paris
entries.gloss: been = went and came back; gone = went and is still there

entries.term: present perfect continuous for duration: I've been waiting for an hour
entries.gloss: an activity that started in the past and is still going on

entries.term: present perfect continuous for a visible result: Have you been running?
entries.gloss: a recent activity explains what we can see or notice now

entries.term: present perfect simple vs. continuous: I've written three emails / I've been writing all day
entries.gloss: simple for completed amounts; continuous for the activity and how long

entries.term: past continuous for an interrupted action: I was cooking when the phone rang
entries.gloss: a longer background action interrupted by a short event in the past simple

entries.term: was going to for a changed plan: I was going to call you, but …
entries.gloss: a past plan or intention that did not happen

entries.term: past perfect for the earlier past: When we arrived, the train had left
entries.gloss: shows that one past event happened before another past event

entries.term: past perfect with by the time: By the time we got there, it had started
entries.gloss: the action was already complete at that past moment

entries.term: will for instant decisions: I'll get the door
entries.gloss: a decision made at the moment of speaking

entries.term: will for offers and promises: I'll send it tonight
entries.gloss: offers and promises about the future; not present simple 'I send it'

entries.term: will for predictions from opinion: I think it'll be fine
entries.gloss: a prediction based on belief, often after I think or probably

entries.term: going to for plans: I'm going to apply for the job
entries.gloss: an intention decided before the moment of speaking

entries.term: going to for predictions from evidence: Look at those clouds, it's going to rain
entries.gloss: a prediction based on what we can see now

entries.term: present continuous for arrangements: I'm meeting Sarah at three
entries.gloss: fixed personal plans, usually with a time and other people

entries.term: present simple for timetables: The train leaves at 6:15
entries.gloss: scheduled events such as transport, classes and programs

entries.term: future continuous for an action in progress: This time tomorrow I'll be flying
entries.gloss: an action that will be in progress at a certain future time

entries.term: future perfect: By Friday, I'll have finished
entries.gloss: an action that will be complete before a certain future time

entries.term: be about to: The meeting is about to start
entries.gloss: something will happen very soon, in the next moments

entries.term: stative verbs: I know / I believe, not 'I'm knowing'
entries.gloss: verbs of knowing, believing, wanting and owning are not used in continuous forms

entries.term: have for possession vs. action: I have a car / I'm having lunch
entries.gloss: have = own is stative; have lunch or a meeting can be continuous

entries.term: think for opinion vs. process: I think so / I'm thinking about it
entries.gloss: think = believe is stative; think = consider can be continuous

entries.term: present simple vs. continuous: I work in Zurich / I'm working from home this week
entries.gloss: simple for permanent situations; continuous for temporary ones

entries.term: gotten as the US past participle: It's gotten worse
entries.gloss: American past participle of get for become, receive or obtain

entries.term: be being + adjective for temporary behavior: You're being rude
entries.gloss: describes how someone is acting now, not a permanent quality

entries.term: just for a very recent action: I've just sent it
entries.gloss: something happened a moment ago; American English also says 'I just sent it'

entries.term: present perfect for news: Scientists have discovered a new species
entries.gloss: announces recent news; the details then follow in the past simple

entries.term: present perfect with an unfinished period: I've had three coffees today
entries.gloss: today, this week and this year are not finished yet

entries.term: the first time + present perfect: It's the first time I've tried this
entries.gloss: not 'It's the first time I try this'

entries.term: present perfect for repeated actions: We've met several times
entries.gloss: how many times up to now, with no finished time

entries.term: haven't … in + period (US): I haven't seen him in years
entries.gloss: American English often uses in instead of for after a negative

entries.term: present perfect continuous with lately: I've been feeling tired lately
entries.gloss: a recent situation that is still going on; also with recently

entries.term: while + past continuous: While I was working, he was sleeping
entries.gloss: two longer actions in progress at the same time in the past

entries.term: when + past simple vs. past continuous: When he arrived, we ate / were eating
entries.gloss: past simple = after he arrived; continuous = already in progress

entries.term: past perfect not needed with before / after: After I finished, I left
entries.gloss: the time word already shows the order, so the past simple is enough

entries.term: when + past simple vs. past perfect: When I arrived, she left / had left
entries.gloss: left = after I arrived; had left = before I arrived

entries.term: past perfect continuous: I had been waiting for an hour when …
entries.gloss: how long an activity went on before a past moment

entries.term: future continuous for polite questions: Will you be using the car tonight?
entries.gloss: asks about someone's plans without sounding like a request

entries.term: hope + present for the future: I hope it goes well
entries.gloss: after hope, the present simple often refers to the future

entries.term: see in simple vs. continuous: I see / I'm seeing a client tomorrow
entries.gloss: I see = I understand; I'm seeing someone = I have a meeting with them

entries.term: senses with can: I can hear music, not 'I'm hearing'
entries.gloss: hear, see and smell usually take can instead of the continuous

entries.term: present continuous for changing situations: Prices are rising
entries.gloss: trends and gradual change happening around now

entries.term: historical present in stories: So I walk in, and he says …
entries.gloss: present tense makes a spoken story or joke more vivid

entries.term: have vs. have got in questions: Do you have a minute? (US)
entries.gloss: American English prefers do you have; have got is more British

entries.term: enjoy / avoid / finish + -ing: I enjoy working here
entries.gloss: these verbs take -ing, never to; not 'enjoy to work'
repeat or continue an action, often an annoying one

entries.term: spend time + -ing: I spent hours fixing it
entries.gloss: not 'spent hours to fix'; also waste time + -ing

entries.term: have trouble + -ing: I had trouble finding it
entries.gloss: have trouble, difficulty or a hard time + -ing
the action is useful or will give a good result

entries.term: decide / plan / hope + to-infinitive: We decided to wait
entries.gloss: these verbs take to + verb, not -ing

entries.term: manage to: I finally managed to fix it
entries.gloss: succeed in doing something difficult

entries.term: tend to: Prices tend to rise in winter
entries.gloss: something usually happens or is generally true

entries.term: stop + -ing vs. stop + to: I stopped smoking / I stopped to smoke
entries.gloss: -ing = quit the activity; to = pause in order to do something

entries.term: remember + -ing vs. remember + to: I remember locking it / Remember to lock it
entries.gloss: -ing = a memory of the past; to = not forget a task

entries.term: forget + to vs. forget + -ing: I forgot to call / I'll never forget meeting her
entries.gloss: to = a task not done; -ing = a past experience

entries.term: try + -ing vs. try + to: Try restarting it / I tried to open it
entries.gloss: -ing = test a method; to = make an effort

entries.term: make someone do: She made me laugh
entries.gloss: make + object + verb without to; force or cause

entries.term: let someone do: Let me know
entries.gloss: allow; let + object + verb without to

entries.term: get someone to do: I got him to help
entries.gloss: persuade someone to do something; get takes to
proposes an action; not 'I suggest to leave'

entries.term: suggest + that-clause, not object + to: I suggest you call her
entries.gloss: not 'I suggest you to call her'; the same with recommend

entries.term: used to + verb: I used to live in Berlin
entries.gloss: a past habit or state that is no longer true

entries.term: be used to + -ing: I'm used to working late
entries.gloss: be familiar with something; to is a preposition here

entries.term: get used to + -ing: You'll get used to driving here
entries.gloss: become familiar with something new over time

entries.term: have something done: I had my hair cut
entries.gloss: someone else does a job or service for you

entries.term: get something done: We need to get the roof fixed
entries.gloss: arrange for a job to be done; also finish a task

entries.term: be interested in + -ing: I'm interested in joining
entries.gloss: preposition + -ing; not 'I'm interested to join the team'

entries.term: think of / about + -ing: I'm thinking of moving
entries.gloss: considering a possible plan; not 'thinking to move'

entries.term: question word + to-infinitive: I don't know what to do
entries.gloss: what, how or where + to + verb for options

entries.term: by + -ing for the method: You save money by cooking at home
entries.gloss: says how something is done or achieved

entries.term: without + -ing: He left without saying goodbye
entries.gloss: the action did not happen; not 'without to say'

entries.term: instead of + -ing: Instead of complaining, do something
entries.gloss: one action replaces another; not 'instead of complain'

entries.term: prevent / stop someone from + -ing: The rain stopped us from going
entries.gloss: keep someone from doing something

entries.term: It's + adjective + to-infinitive: It's hard to say
entries.gloss: it stands for the to-clause; a common way to comment

entries.term: have someone do (US): I'll have her call you
entries.gloss: ask or arrange for someone to do a task; common at work

entries.term: it takes + time + to: It took me an hour to get here
entries.gloss: says how much time someone needs to do something
think about a possible action; not 'consider to move'

entries.term: regret + -ing vs. regret + to: I regret saying that / I regret to say …
entries.gloss: -ing = sorry about the past; to = a formal way to give bad news

entries.term: go on + -ing vs. go on + to: She went on talking / She went on to become CEO
entries.gloss: -ing = continue the same thing; to = do something next

entries.term: mean + -ing vs. mean + to: It means waiting / I didn't mean to hurt you
entries.gloss: -ing = involve as a result; to = intend

entries.term: need + -ing with passive meaning: The car needs washing
entries.gloss: same as 'needs to be washed', which Americans usually prefer

entries.term: like + to-infinitive or -ing: I like to cook / I like cooking
entries.gloss: both are correct; American English often prefers to

entries.term: would rather + bare infinitive: I'd rather stay in
entries.gloss: prefer to do something; no to after would rather

entries.term: help + infinitive with or without to: She helped me move
entries.gloss: to is optional; American English usually drops it

entries.term: see / hear someone do vs. doing: I saw him leave / leaving
entries.gloss: bare verb = the whole action; -ing = part of an action in progress

entries.term: didn't use to: I didn't use to like coffee
entries.gloss: after did, write use, not used, in negatives and questions

entries.term: usually for present habits: I usually walk, not 'I use to walk'
entries.gloss: used to is only for the past; present habits take usually

entries.term: have something done for bad experiences: I had my phone stolen
entries.gloss: something bad happened to you, done by another person

entries.term: to as a preposition + -ing: We're committed to improving
entries.gloss: after object to or be committed to, -ing follows to

entries.term: It's + adjective + for someone + to: It's hard for me to say
entries.gloss: for + person names who the comment is about

entries.term: find it + adjective + to: I find it hard to focus
entries.gloss: it is needed; not 'I find hard to focus'

entries.term: adjective + to-infinitive for reactions: I was surprised to hear that
entries.gloss: a feeling about an event: happy to help, sorry to hear

entries.term: how about / what about + -ing: How about meeting on Friday?
entries.gloss: makes a suggestion; -ing or a noun follows about

entries.term: good at + -ing: She's good at explaining things
entries.gloss: adjective + preposition + -ing; not 'good in explaining'

parts.title: Conditionals, passives & reported speech
parts.deck: kizamu-english::C1::10 Grammar::03 Conditionals, passives & reported speech

entries.term: first conditional: If it rains, we'll stay in
entries.gloss: real future possibility; present after if, not 'if it will rain'

entries.term: second conditional: If I had more time, I'd travel
entries.gloss: unreal present or unlikely future; past after if, would in the result

entries.term: past, not would, after if: If I knew, I'd tell you
entries.gloss: in unreal conditions use the past after if, not 'if I would know'

entries.term: third conditional: If I had known, I would have come
entries.gloss: unreal past; avoid 'if I would have known' in writing

entries.term: first vs. second conditional: If I get the job / If I got the job
entries.gloss: first = realistic; second = unlikely or only imagined

entries.term: present simple passive: Coffee is grown in Brazil
entries.gloss: facts and processes when the doer is unknown or unimportant

entries.term: past simple passive: The bridge was built in 1890
entries.gloss: past events where the result matters more than the doer

entries.term: present perfect passive: The meeting has been canceled
entries.gloss: recent changes or news without naming who did it

entries.term: present continuous passive: The room is being cleaned
entries.gloss: an action happening to something right now

entries.term: future passive: The results will be announced on Monday
entries.gloss: future events in official plans and announcements

entries.term: passive with modals: It must be done today
entries.gloss: modal + be + past participle: can be found, should be checked

entries.term: passive with two objects: I was given a laptop
entries.gloss: the person usually becomes the subject: I was told, I was offered
informal passive for changes, often sudden or bad: got hired, got hurt

entries.term: reported statements with backshift: She said she was tired
entries.gloss: after a past reporting verb, the tense usually moves back

entries.term: will becomes would in reported speech: She said she'd call
entries.gloss: a reported promise or prediction uses would

entries.term: no backshift for things still true: He said he lives in Boston
entries.gloss: keep the present if it is still true now

entries.term: reported yes/no questions with if or whether: She asked if I was ready
entries.gloss: no do or did, and statement word order

entries.term: reported wh-questions: He asked where I lived
entries.gloss: statement word order; not 'he asked where did I live'

entries.term: reported commands with tell: She told me to wait
entries.gloss: tell + person + to-infinitive

entries.term: reported negative commands: He told me not to worry
entries.gloss: not before to; not 'he told me don't worry'

entries.term: reported requests with ask: I asked her to send it
entries.gloss: ask + person + to-infinitive for polite requests

entries.term: zero conditional: If you heat ice, it melts
entries.gloss: general truths and results that always happen; present in both clauses

entries.term: first conditional with an imperative: If you see her, tell her
entries.gloss: an instruction that depends on a possible situation

entries.term: second conditional with could / might: If I had a car, I could drive you
entries.gloss: could = would be able to; might = would possibly

entries.term: third conditional with could / might: If we'd left earlier, we might have made it
entries.gloss: a possible, not certain, different past result

entries.term: 'd = had or would: If I'd known, I'd have called
entries.gloss: after if, 'd means had; in the result clause it means would

entries.term: unless without a second negative: Unless you hurry, you'll miss it
entries.gloss: unless already means 'if not'; not 'unless you don't hurry'

entries.term: past perfect passive: The files had already been deleted
entries.gloss: something done to something before another past event

entries.term: modal perfect passive: It should have been done yesterday
entries.gloss: criticism or deduction about a past action done to something

entries.term: by + agent in the passive: It was written by Toni Morrison
entries.gloss: add by only when the doer is important or new information

entries.term: passive infinitive: The report needs to be finished
entries.gloss: to be + past participle after need, want or have to

entries.term: passive -ing form: I hate being interrupted
entries.gloss: being + past participle after verbs and prepositions

entries.term: be born: I was born in 1990
entries.gloss: always past passive for birth; not 'I am born in 1990'

entries.term: passive with prepositional verbs: The problem was dealt with
entries.gloss: the preposition stays after the verb: was looked after, was paid for

entries.term: past events → past perfect in reported speech: He said he had finished
entries.gloss: reported earlier events move back to the past perfect

entries.term: no backshift after a present reporting verb: She says she's busy
entries.gloss: after says or has said, the tense does not change

entries.term: modals in reported speech: can → could, must → had to
entries.gloss: can, will and must usually move back; could and should stay

entries.term: backshift after thought and knew: I thought you were coming
entries.gloss: a past thinking verb moves the following clause back

entries.term: deny + -ing: He denied taking the money
entries.gloss: say that you did not do something

entries.term: admit + -ing: She admitted making a mistake
entries.gloss: agree that something bad is true, often unwillingly

entries.term: refuse to: They refused to pay
entries.gloss: say that you will not do something

entries.term: promise to: He promised to call back
entries.gloss: say that you will certainly do something

entries.term: warn someone not to: She warned us not to go
entries.gloss: tell someone about a danger so they avoid it

entries.term: offer to: She offered to help
entries.gloss: the speaker will do it; not 'she offered me to help'

entries.term: accuse someone of + -ing: They accused him of lying
entries.gloss: say that someone did something wrong

entries.term: apologize for + -ing: He apologized for being late
entries.gloss: say sorry; for + -ing, not a to-infinitive

entries.term: advise someone to: The doctor advised me to rest
entries.gloss: recommend an action to someone

entries.term: remind someone to: She reminded me to call
entries.gloss: help someone remember a task; remind + person + to

entries.term: first conditional with a modal: If you finish early, you can go
entries.gloss: can, may or should in the result clause instead of will

entries.term: passive questions: When was it built?
entries.gloss: question word + be + subject + past participle; not 'When it was built?'

entries.term: defining relative clause: the woman who called
entries.gloss: identifies which person or thing; no commas

entries.term: non-defining relative clause: My sister, who lives in Ohio, …
entries.gloss: extra information between commas; who or which, never that

entries.term: leaving out the object pronoun: the book I read
entries.gloss: the object relative pronoun is often dropped, especially in speech

entries.term: no extra pronoun in relative clauses: the book that I bought
entries.gloss: not 'the book that I bought it'

entries.term: where in relative clauses: the city where I grew up
entries.gloss: where = in which, after place nouns

entries.term: although / even though + clause: Although it was late, we kept going
entries.gloss: contrast with a full clause; even though is stronger

entries.term: despite / in spite of + noun: Despite the rain, we went
entries.gloss: followed by a noun, not a full clause like although

entries.term: despite + -ing: Despite feeling sick, she came
entries.gloss: the subject of the -ing form is the subject of the main clause

entries.term: however as a connector: It's expensive. However, it works.
entries.gloss: starts a new sentence with a comma; not used like but

entries.term: to-infinitive of purpose: I came to see you
entries.gloss: says why; not 'for see' or 'for to see'

entries.term: in order to: We cut costs in order to survive
entries.gloss: purpose; more formal than to alone

entries.term: so that + can / could: I left early so that I could catch the train
entries.gloss: purpose, often with a new subject or a modal

entries.term: because vs. because of: because it rained / because of the rain
entries.gloss: because + clause; because of + noun

entries.term: due to + noun: The delay was due to the weather
entries.gloss: because of; common in news and official language

entries.term: so vs. such: so tired / such a long day
entries.gloss: so + adjective; such (a) + adjective + noun

entries.term: too vs. not enough: too small / not big enough
entries.gloss: too = more than needed; not enough = less than needed

entries.term: position of enough: enough time / good enough
entries.gloss: enough comes before nouns but after adjectives and adverbs

entries.term: either … or: either today or tomorrow
entries.gloss: one of two choices

entries.term: not only … but also without inversion: She not only wrote it but also directed it
entries.gloss: adds a second point with normal word order inside the sentence

entries.term: present tense after when / as soon as: I'll call you when I get home
entries.gloss: future meaning; not 'when I will get home'

entries.term: who for people, which for things: the man who / the box which
entries.gloss: not 'the book who'; that is possible for both in defining clauses

entries.term: subject relative pronoun cannot be dropped: the man who called me
entries.gloss: not 'the man called me' when the pronoun is the subject

entries.term: whose as a possessive relative: the colleague whose laptop broke
entries.gloss: replaces his, her or their in a relative clause

entries.term: where vs. which for places: the town where I live / the town I visited
entries.gloss: where replaces in which; a verb with a direct object needs which or that

entries.term: when in relative clauses: the day when we met
entries.gloss: when = on which, after time nouns; often left out

entries.term: what as a relative pronoun: I did what you asked
entries.gloss: what = the thing that; not 'that what' or 'which'

entries.term: despite the fact that + clause: despite the fact that it rained
entries.gloss: despite needs 'the fact that' before a full clause

entries.term: however in the middle: The plan, however, failed
entries.gloss: however between commas inside the sentence

entries.term: nevertheless / nonetheless: The risk is high; nevertheless, we'll try
entries.gloss: formal 'but still'; in spite of what was just said

entries.term: while meaning although: While I agree, I have some doubts
entries.gloss: admits one point before a contrasting point

entries.term: yet as a conjunction: simple yet effective
entries.gloss: but; adds a surprising contrast, often between adjectives

entries.term: so as not to / in order not to: so as not to wake her
entries.gloss: negative purpose; more formal than 'to not'

entries.term: for + noun for purpose: We went out for dinner
entries.gloss: for + noun, not for + verb, to say why

entries.term: since / as for reasons: Since you're here, you can help
entries.gloss: gives a known reason, usually at the start of the sentence

entries.term: so … that / such … that for results: It was so cold that we stayed in
entries.gloss: a strong degree and its result

entries.term: so much / so many + noun: so many people
entries.gloss: not 'such many people'; with nouns use so much or so many

entries.term: too … to: too tired to drive
entries.gloss: the degree makes the action impossible

entries.term: both … and: both fast and cheap
entries.gloss: two things are true together

entries.term: neither … nor: neither fast nor cheap
entries.gloss: not one and not the other; no extra not in the sentence

entries.term: as soon as + present perfect: as soon as I've finished
entries.gloss: the first action will be complete before the next one

entries.term: by the time + present for the future: By the time you arrive, I'll have left
entries.gloss: present after by the time; future perfect in the main clause

entries.term: once meaning as soon as: Once you've signed, we can start
entries.gloss: after something is done or happens

entries.term: before / after + -ing: Before leaving, check the lights
entries.gloss: -ing after these prepositions when the subject is the same

entries.term: apart from: Apart from John, everyone came
entries.gloss: except for; also means 'in addition to'

entries.term: no but after although: Although it was late, we stayed
entries.gloss: not 'Although it was late, but we stayed'

entries.term: rather than + verb: Let's walk rather than drive
entries.gloss: prefers one action to another

entries.term: so that vs. so: I left early so that I could rest / It rained, so we stayed
entries.gloss: so that = purpose; so alone = result

entries.term: adjective + that-clause: I'm sure it'll work
entries.gloss: that is often dropped after sure, glad, afraid and sorry

entries.term: after that / afterward: After that, we had dinner
entries.gloss: after alone needs a noun or clause; afterward is the American adverb

entries.term: everything that, not everything what: Everything she said was true
entries.gloss: after everything, all and nothing use that or no pronoun, not what

parts.title: Articles, quantifiers, modals & comparison
parts.deck: kizamu-english::C1::10 Grammar::05 Articles, quantifiers, modals & comparison

entries.term: a / an for first mention, the for second: I saw a dog. The dog …
entries.gloss: new information takes a or an; known information takes the

entries.term: a / an with jobs: She's an engineer
entries.gloss: not 'She's engineer'; a singular job needs a or an

entries.term: how much vs. how many: how much time / how many people
entries.gloss: much with uncountable nouns; many with plural nouns

entries.term: a lot vs. a lot of: I like it a lot / a lot of people
entries.gloss: of only when a noun follows

entries.term: some in offers and requests: Would you like some coffee?
entries.gloss: some in questions when you expect or want the answer yes

entries.term: any in questions and negatives: Do you have any questions?
entries.gloss: any in open questions and after not

entries.term: no double negative: I didn't see anyone
entries.gloss: not 'I didn't see nobody'; use any- after not

entries.term: another vs. other vs. the others: another coffee / other people / the others
entries.gloss: another + singular; other + plural; the others = the rest

entries.term: must vs. have to: I must go / I have to go
entries.gloss: must = the speaker's own feeling; have to = a rule; US prefers have to

entries.term: don't have to vs. mustn't: You don't have to come / You mustn't tell anyone
entries.gloss: not necessary vs. not allowed

entries.term: had to for past obligation: I had to work late
entries.gloss: must has no past form; use had to

entries.term: should for advice: You should see a doctor
entries.gloss: advice or a recommendation; ought to is more formal

entries.term: must be for present deduction: She must be tired
entries.gloss: an almost certain conclusion from evidence

entries.term: can't be for present deduction: That can't be right
entries.gloss: you are sure something is impossible or not true

entries.term: might / may / could be: He might be in a meeting
entries.gloss: present possibility: perhaps it is true

entries.term: Can I / Could I / May I for permission: Could I borrow your pen?
entries.gloss: could is more polite than can; may is formal

entries.term: Could you / Would you for requests: Could you send me the file?
entries.gloss: polite requests; can you is more informal

entries.term: much / far / a lot + comparative: much better, far more expensive
entries.gloss: makes a comparison stronger; not 'very better'

entries.term: a bit / slightly + comparative: a bit cheaper, slightly higher
entries.gloss: shows that the difference is small

entries.term: as … as: as fast as / just as good as
entries.gloss: equal comparison; as, not than, after the adjective

entries.term: not as … as: It's not as hard as I thought
entries.gloss: less than; often more natural than 'less … than'

entries.term: superlative + ever with present perfect: the best movie I've ever seen
entries.gloss: superlative followed by ever, usually with the present perfect

entries.term: no double comparative: cheaper, not 'more cheaper'
entries.gloss: short adjectives take -er; long ones take more

entries.term: one of the + superlative + plural: one of the best restaurants
entries.gloss: the noun after one of the is plural

entries.term: question tags: It's late, isn't it?
entries.gloss: positive statement + negative tag; negative statement + positive tag

entries.term: indirect questions: Could you tell me where the station is?
entries.gloss: statement word order after a polite opening

entries.term: indirect yes/no questions: Do you know if she's here?
entries.gloss: if or whether, then statement word order

entries.term: subject vs. object questions: Who called you? / Who did you call?
entries.gloss: no do when who or what is the subject

entries.term: might / may for future possibility: I might come later
entries.gloss: perhaps it will happen; might is more common in speech

entries.term: the for things both speakers know: Can you close the door?
entries.gloss: the when the listener knows which one you mean

entries.term: no article with meals, sports and languages: have lunch, play tennis
entries.gloss: not 'have the lunch' or 'speak the German'

entries.term: a / an for rates and frequency: twice a week, $20 an hour
entries.gloss: a or an means per

entries.term: no article before next / last + time: next week, last year
entries.gloss: next week, last month and this year need no article or preposition

entries.term: plenty of: We have plenty of time
entries.gloss: more than enough; with plural and uncountable nouns

entries.term: no + noun vs. not any: There's no milk / There isn't any milk
entries.gloss: the same meaning; no sounds stronger

entries.term: each vs. every: each of us / every day
entries.gloss: each = one by one, also for two; every = all of three or more

entries.term: too much / too many: too much work / too many emails
entries.gloss: more than is good; much for uncountable, many for plural

entries.term: don't need to for no necessity: You don't need to bring anything
entries.gloss: not necessary; American English rarely uses needn't

entries.term: be supposed to for rules: You're not supposed to park here
entries.gloss: what a rule or other people expect you to do

entries.term: can't for rules: You can't park here
entries.gloss: not allowed; much more common than mustn't in American English

entries.term: be able to in other forms: will be able to, have been able to
entries.gloss: can has no future or perfect form, so use be able to

entries.term: twice as … as: twice as expensive as
entries.gloss: multiples: three times as big as, half as much as

entries.term: comparative and comparative: better and better, more and more
entries.gloss: shows a change that continues over time

entries.term: different from / different than (US): It's different than I expected
entries.gloss: different than is normal in American English; from is safe everywhere

entries.term: much too + adjective: much too expensive
entries.gloss: strengthens too; not 'too much expensive'

entries.term: question tag after I'm: I'm late, aren't I?
entries.gloss: the tag for I am is aren't I

entries.term: answering negative questions: You're not coming? No, I'm not.
entries.gloss: yes or no follows the true answer, not the question

entries.term: position of all and both: We all agreed / They're both busy
entries.gloss: before the main verb, but after be and auxiliaries

entries.term: which vs. what in questions: Which one do you want?
entries.gloss: which for a limited choice; what for an open choice

entries.term: one / ones as a substitute: I'll take the blue one
entries.gloss: replaces a countable noun so you do not repeat it
